title: Bitter, black and global
text: Coffee supports a supply chain of {{1}} proportions: some 125 million people earn their living from it, most of them smallholder farmers tending a few hectares of volcanic hillside. The plant is {{2}} fussy — it grows in a narrow band of altitude and warmth, which is why the drink carries the names of mountains and regions in a way wheat never does. The economics are notoriously {{3}}: farmers receive a small share of the retail price, and world-market prices {{4}} so wildly that a bad year can wipe out a family's income. The industry's {{5}} has been to certify: schemes promise premiums for shade-grown or fairly traded beans, though auditors debate how much reaches the {{6}}. Meanwhile consumption keeps {{7}}: the drink that fuelled the Enlightenment now fuels the morning commute, and cafes have {{8}} into the default offices of the freelance age. From Ethiopian goats to laptop lattes, coffee has always sold the same thing — alertness, sociability and the illusion of a slower morning.

gaps.explanation: 'a supply chain of industrial proportions' — enormous, like heavy industry; industrious = hard-working.
'the plant is notoriously fussy' — famously so; erroneously = mistakenly.
'the economics are notoriously unstable' — liable to collapse; unstinting = generous without limit.
'prices fluctuate so wildly' — the standard verb for irregular price movement; flounder = struggle helplessly.
'the industry's response has been to certify' — its answer to the problem; residue = what is left behind.
'how much reaches the growers' — the people who farm the beans; grocer = a food retailer.
'consumption keeps spreading' — continuing to extend; shun = deliberately avoid.
'cafes have morphed into the default offices' — transformed gradually; moor = tie up a boat.
